title: Quiz 2: Features, Preprocessing and Dimensionality
description: 141 questions on features and feature types, missing data, imputation, binning, encoding, scaling, validation, the curse of dimensionality, feature selection and PCA (with short-answer practice).

questions.question: In a dataset used for machine learning, what is a feature?
options: One measurable input column that describes each example
One finished model that has been trained on every example
One summary row that lists the average of every column
One outcome column that the model is built to predict
questions.explanation: Features are the inputs, one per column. The thing being predicted is the target.

questions.question: Which of these is a continuous quantitative feature?
options: A patient's number of previous hospital visits this year
A patient's body temperature measured to a tenth of a degree
A patient's pain rating of mild, moderate or severe
A patient's blood type, such as A, B, AB or O
questions.explanation: A continuous feature can take any value in a range, including decimals. Visit counts are discrete, the pain rating is ordinal and blood type is nominal.

questions.question: A column records how many items each customer bought, always a whole number. What type of feature is it?
options: Continuous quantitative: any value on a smooth scale
Ordinal qualitative: ranked categories with named levels
Discrete quantitative: countable whole-number amounts
Nominal qualitative: unordered categories with no ranking
questions.explanation: Counts are numbers you can add and average, but they jump in whole steps, so they are discrete.

questions.question: What makes a feature ordinal rather than nominal?
options: Its categories are numbers, so the gaps between them are measured exactly
Its categories are text labels, so they can be sorted alphabetically
Its categories are few in number, so they can be listed on a short chart
Its categories have a meaningful order, though the gaps between them are not measured
questions.explanation: Ordinal means ranked (small, medium, large). Nominal means named with no ranking (red, green, blue). Alphabetical order is not a meaningful order.

questions.question: Which feature is ordinal?
options: Shirt size recorded as small, medium, large or extra large
Favourite colour recorded as red, green, blue or yellow
Home country recorded as Canada, Japan, Brazil or Kenya
Pet type recorded as dog, cat, rabbit or goldfish
questions.explanation: Sizes rank from small to extra large. The others are names with no natural order (nominal).

questions.question: A dataset stores postal codes such as 90210 and 10001 as numbers. How should the feature be treated?
options: As continuous: the codes are numbers, so averages of them are meaningful
As nominal: the codes name places, so arithmetic on them has no meaning
As discrete quantitative: the codes are whole numbers, so sums of them are useful
As ordinal: the codes can be sorted, so larger codes mean a larger place
questions.explanation: A number used as a label is still a category. Adding two postal codes or calling one 'bigger' tells you nothing.

questions.question: Qualitative features describe categories or qualities rather than measured amounts.
questions.explanation: Qualitative (categorical) features are nominal or ordinal. Quantitative features are measured amounts.

questions.question: A nominal feature has a natural order from lowest to highest.
questions.explanation: Nominal categories are only names. Categories with an order are ordinal.

questions.question: Match each feature to its type.
A categorical feature whose values have a natural order, such as low, medium and high, is called ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Ordinal categories rank in order; nominal categories do not.

questions.question: In pandas, what does NaN stand for in a column?
options: A real number that is stored when a value is exactly zero
A label that is stored when a category has been left blank
A placeholder marking a value that is missing or undefined
A warning that is stored when a value is far outside the range
questions.explanation: NaN means 'not a number' and is how pandas marks a missing value. Zero is a real value, not a gap.

questions.question: Which expression gives the number of missing values in each column of a DataFrame df?
options: df.dropna().sum()
df.fillna().count()
df.describe().isna()
df.isna().sum()
questions.explanation: isna() marks each missing cell as True, and sum() counts the True values per column.

questions.question: What does df.dropna() do when called with no arguments?
options: Removes every row that has a missing value in any column
Removes every column that has a missing value in any row
Removes only the rows where every column is missing a value
Removes only the cells that are missing and shifts the rest up
questions.explanation: By default dropna() works on rows (axis=0) and drops a row if any of its values is NaN.

questions.question: What does df.dropna(axis=1) do?
options: Removes every row that contains at least one missing value
Removes every column that contains at least one missing value
Removes the first column whether or not it has missing values
Removes every column in which all of the values are missing
questions.explanation: axis=1 switches the direction from rows to columns.

questions.question: When is dropping the rows that have missing values a reasonable choice?
options: A large share of rows have gaps and few complete rows remain
Every row has a gap in the same column and that column matters
A small share of rows have gaps and plenty of complete rows remain
The gaps follow a pattern and are tied to the outcome being predicted
questions.explanation: Removal is simple and safe when it throws away little data and the gaps are not systematic.

questions.question: When is dropping a whole column a sensible way to handle missing data?
options: Most of its values are present, so it can offer the model a great deal
A few of its values are missing, so the rows can be left in place instead
All of its values are numeric, so it can be filled with a single average
Most of its values are missing, so it can offer the model very little
questions.explanation: A column that is mostly empty carries little information, and filling it would mean inventing most of it.

questions.question: A table has 1,000 rows and 5 feature columns. Each column is missing about 4% of its values, in different rows. What is likely after df.dropna()?
options: Much more than 4% of the rows are lost, because one gap anywhere removes the row
Exactly 4% of the rows are lost, because each column loses 4% of its values
Fewer than 4% of the rows are lost, because the gaps overlap in the same rows
No rows are lost, because dropna() only removes the single missing cell
questions.explanation: Gaps in different columns add up across rows. With 5 columns at 4% each, roughly 18% of the rows have at least one gap.

questions.question: Removing rows with missing values can bias a model if the values are not missing at random.
questions.explanation: If, for example, high earners skip an income question, dropping those rows leaves a sample that no longer represents everyone.

questions.question: Dropping rows and dropping columns are two different removal methods.
questions.explanation: Rows are removed with dropna(); columns can be removed with dropna(axis=1) or by dropping the column by name.

questions.question: The pandas method that removes rows containing missing values is called ____. (one word, no brackets)
questions.explanation: df.dropna() removes rows with any NaN.

questions.question: A survey table has 20% of its rows with at least one missing value, and one column that is 90% empty. Describe how you would use removal methods on this data and justify each choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Drop the 90% empty column: it carries almost no information and filling it would mean inventing most of its values. Then look at the rows. If the remaining gaps are scattered and 20% of rows can be spared, dropna() on rows is simple. If losing a fifth of the data hurts, or the gaps are tied to the outcome, fill the values instead of deleting.
rubric: Drops the mostly empty column and gives the reason (almost no information)
Considers dropping the incomplete rows with dropna() and states a condition (the loss is small and not systematic)
Mentions the risk of bias or lost data when many rows are removed
Names filling the gaps (imputation) as the alternative

questions.question: What is imputation?
options: Removing the rows with missing values rather than estimating them
Filling in missing values with estimated ones rather than removing the rows
Converting the missing values into a column of text labels
Rescaling the existing values so that the gaps no longer show
questions.explanation: Imputation keeps the row and replaces each gap with a sensible estimate.

questions.question: A column holds 10, 12, 14, 40 and one NaN. What does a mean fill put in the gap?
A column holds 10, 12, 14, 40 and one NaN. What does a median fill put in the gap?
questions.explanation: The four values in order are 10, 12, 14, 40. The middle two are 12 and 14, and their average is 13.

questions.question: A salary column has a few extremely large values. Which fill is usually safer, and why?
options: The median, because extreme values do not pull it the way they pull the mean
The mean, because extreme values are the best guide to a typical salary
The mode, because every salary appears the same number of times
The maximum, because the gap is most likely to hold a large salary
questions.explanation: The median depends on the middle of the sorted data, so a few extreme values barely move it.

questions.question: A column holds 3, 5, 5, 7, 5 and one NaN. What does a mode fill put in the gap?
questions.explanation: The mode is the most frequent value, and 5 appears three times.

questions.question: What is a missing indicator?
options: A new row at the bottom of the table that counts the gaps in each column
A new error message that stops the program when a gap is found in the data
A new 0/1 column that records which rows had a missing value before filling
A new filled value that is chosen at random from the other rows in the column
questions.explanation: The indicator is kept next to the filled column so the model can still tell which values were guesses.

questions.question: Why might you add a missing indicator along with a numerical fill?
options: Because the filled value is always exactly equal to the true value
Because the model cannot run unless every column has a twin column
Because the indicator replaces the need to fill the original column
Because the fact that a value was missing can itself be informative
questions.explanation: For example, a blank income answer may signal something about the person. The indicator keeps that signal.

questions.question: What is the risk of filling every gap in an age column with the constant 0?
options: Zero looks like a real age, so it can distort the distribution and mislead the model
Zero is not a number, so pandas refuses to store it in a numeric column
Zero is always larger than the true age, so every prediction is pushed up
Zero removes the row from the table, so the number of examples falls
questions.explanation: A constant is easy to apply but can be mistaken for real data. A value such as -1 plus a missing indicator is clearer.

questions.question: Filling gaps with the column's mean leaves the column's mean unchanged.
questions.explanation: Adding values equal to the mean does not move the average.

questions.question: Filling gaps with the column's mean also leaves the column's spread (variance) unchanged.
questions.explanation: Every filled value sits at the centre, so the spread shrinks. Heavy mean filling makes the column look less variable than it really is.

questions.question: A numeric column contains a few huge outliers. The fill that is least affected by them is the ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value, so extremes do not move it.

questions.question: A column of favourite colours has gaps. Which numerical fill cannot be used on it?
options: Mode fill, because words have no most frequent entry
Mean fill, because words have no average
Constant fill, because words cannot be stored as a fixed value
Missing indicator, because words cannot be flagged as absent
questions.explanation: You cannot average words. The mode, a constant such as 'Unknown' and a missing indicator all work on categories.

questions.question: What does a mode fill do to a categorical column?
options: Puts the category that appears least often into every gap
Puts a random category chosen from the column into every gap
Puts the most common category into every gap
Puts the category from the neighbouring row into every gap
questions.explanation: In pandas: df['city'].fillna(df['city'].mode()[0]).

questions.question: A column holds Red, NaN, NaN, Blue in row order. What does a forward fill give?
options: Red, Blue, Blue, Blue
Red, Red, Blue, Blue
Blue, Red, Red, Blue
Red, Red, Red, Blue
questions.explanation: Forward fill copies the last known value downward into each gap.

questions.question: A column holds Red, NaN, NaN, Blue in row order. What does a backfill give?
options: Red, Blue, Blue, Blue
Red, Red, Red, Blue
Red, Red, Blue, Blue
Blue, Red, Red, Blue
questions.explanation: Backfill copies the next known value upward into each gap.

questions.question: In pandas, which fill method name means the same thing as forward fill?
options: bfill
pad
mode
interpolate
questions.explanation: 'pad' and 'ffill' both propagate the last valid value forward. 'bfill' and 'backfill' go the other way.

questions.question: When is forward fill or backfill a poor choice?
options: The rows are in time order, so the neighbouring row is a sensible guess
The column is categorical, so the neighbouring row is a different type
The rows have no meaningful order, so the neighbouring row is an arbitrary guess
The gaps are short, so the neighbouring row is only one step away
questions.explanation: These methods suit ordered data such as daily records. In shuffled data the row above says nothing about the missing value.

questions.question: You fill every gap in a 'payment method' column with the new label 'Unknown'. Which method is this?
options: Mode fill, using the most common category in the column
Backfill, using the next known value from the rows below
Missing indicator, using a separate 0/1 column for the gaps
Constant fill, using a fixed label instead of a real category
questions.explanation: A fixed value is a constant fill. It also acts as a missing flag inside the column, because 'Unknown' marks where data was absent.

questions.question: After a forward fill, a missing value in the very first row is still missing.
questions.explanation: There is no earlier value to copy. A backfill, or a different method, is needed for that row.

questions.question: Match each categorical fill to what it does.

pairs.right: Uses one fixed label such as 'Unknown'

questions.question: Filling a categorical gap with the most frequent category is called ____ fill. (one word)
questions.explanation: The mode is the most frequent value.

questions.question: A column of customer 'region' values has 8% missing entries. Describe two different ways to fill it and one weakness of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Mode fill puts the most common region into every gap. It is quick, but it makes the most common region look even more common and can bury real differences. Constant fill (or a missing indicator) labels the gaps 'Unknown' or adds a 0/1 flag. It keeps the information that a value was missing, but 'Unknown' becomes an extra category the model has to handle, and the gaps are not turned into real regions.
rubric: Describes one valid fill (mode, constant, forward/backfill or missing indicator)
Describes a second, different valid fill
Gives a genuine weakness for the first method
Gives a genuine weakness for the second method

questions.question: What is discretization?
options: Turning a continuous numeric feature into a small set of ranges or categories
Turning a categorical feature into one 0/1 column for each category
Turning a raw feature into a standard scale with the same average
Turning a table with gaps into one with every missing value filled
questions.explanation: Binning is the common way to discretize: each value is replaced by the bin it falls into.

questions.question: How does equal-width binning choose its bins?
options: Each bin holds the same number of values, whatever size of range it covers
Each bin covers the same size of range, whatever number of values fall inside
Each bin is centred on the average value, whatever size of range it covers
Each bin is chosen by a person, whatever size of range the values cover
questions.explanation: Width = (max - min) / number of bins. Counts per bin can then differ a lot.

questions.question: How does equal-frequency binning choose its bins?
options: Each bin covers exactly the same size of range, so the counts can differ
Each bin is placed at a fixed spacing of ten, so the counts can differ
Each bin holds roughly the same number of values, so the ranges can differ
Each bin is formed from the rows that share a category, so the sizes can differ
questions.explanation: Frequency bins are cut at quantiles, so each bin contains about the same number of rows.

questions.question: A feature runs from 10 to 70 and is cut into 3 equal-width bins. Which bin does the value 45 fall in?
questions.explanation: Width = (70 - 10) / 3 = 20, so the bins are 10 to 30, 30 to 50 and 50 to 70.

questions.question: The values are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 100. They are cut into 2 equal-width bins. How many values land in the upper bin?
questions.explanation: Width = 99 / 2 = 49.5, so the bins are 1 to 50.5 and 50.5 to 100. Only the outlier 100 reaches the upper bin.

questions.question: The values are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 100. They are cut into 2 equal-frequency bins. Which values share the upper bin?
options: 7 and 100
100 alone
questions.explanation: Equal frequency puts 4 values in each bin: 1 to 4 in the lower bin and 5, 6, 7 and 100 in the upper.

questions.question: Which statement about outliers and binning is correct?
options: Equal-frequency bins can be crowded by an outlier, but equal-width bins stay balanced
Both kinds of bins grow wider to hold an outlier, and each stays equally balanced
Equal-width bins can be crowded by an outlier, but equal-frequency bins stay balanced
Neither kind of bin is affected by an outlier, because binning ignores the actual values
questions.explanation: One extreme value stretches the range, so equal-width bins leave most values in a few bins. Equal-frequency bins are cut by rank.

questions.question: In pandas, which function makes equal-frequency bins?
options: pd.cut()
pd.bin()
pd.round()
pd.qcut()
questions.explanation: qcut cuts at quantiles (equal frequency). cut() uses equal-width bins unless you pass the edges yourself.

questions.question: A 'minutes watched' column is turned into 'long' (30 minutes or more) and 'short' (under 30) using one cut-off. What is this called?
options: Binarization: a threshold splits a continuous value into two groups
Standardization: a mean and spread turn a continuous value into a z-score
One-hot encoding: a column per category turns a label into several columns
Forward fill: a neighbouring row turns a missing value into a copied value
questions.explanation: Binarization is binning with a single threshold, so every value lands in one of two groups.

questions.question: How does binarization differ from equal-width binning?
options: It uses several chosen thresholds and gives many groups, rather than two same-size ranges
It uses one chosen threshold and gives two groups, rather than several same-size ranges
It uses the column average as the cut and gives equal counts, rather than same-size ranges
It uses the target as the cut and gives one group per class, rather than same-size ranges
questions.explanation: The threshold is a judgement call, such as 5,000 views for 'popular'. Equal-width bins are computed from the min, max and number of bins.

questions.question: Binning loses detail, because values inside the same bin become identical.
questions.explanation: That is the trade-off: a simpler, less noisy feature at the cost of some precision.

questions.question: Binning is an example of discretization.
questions.explanation: Discretization is the general idea of turning continuous values into a limited set of categories; binning is how.

questions.question: Splitting a range into bins of the same size, whatever their counts, is called equal-____ binning. (one word)
questions.explanation: Equal-width bins have the same range; equal-frequency bins have the same count.

questions.question: Why must categorical features be encoded before most models can use them?
options: The algorithms refuse text for security reasons, so all data must be anonymous
The algorithms run faster on text, so all data must be converted back later
The algorithms do arithmetic on the inputs, so all data must ultimately be numeric
The algorithms need every column to match, so all data must have the same length
questions.explanation: Distances, weights and sums need numbers. Text categories must be turned into numbers first.

questions.question: How is a binary feature such as 'subscribed' (yes or no) usually encoded?
options: As one column of -1, 0 and 1
As two columns of words
As one column of 1 to 10
As one column of 0 and 1
questions.explanation: Two values map to 0 and 1.

questions.question: When is one-hot encoding the right choice?
options: A nominal feature has three or more categories with no natural order
A nominal feature has exactly two categories with no natural order
An ordinal feature has three or more categories with a natural order
A continuous feature has many distinct values with a natural order
questions.explanation: Two categories need only a binary column. Ordered categories can keep their order as numbers.

questions.question: Why is it a problem to encode red, green and blue as 1, 2 and 3?
options: It makes the column too small, so the model has too few values to learn from
It tells the model that blue is greater than red and sits twice as far away
It makes the column non-numeric, so the model cannot use any of its values
It makes the colours random, so the model sees a different order every run
questions.explanation: The numbers invent an order and distances that the colours do not have.

questions.question: A 'city' feature has 12 distinct values. How many new columns does one-hot encoding create?
questions.explanation: One 0/1 column per category. (Some tools offer to drop one, since it can be worked out from the others.)

questions.question: What does target encoding do?
options: Replaces each category with the number of times that category appears in the data
Replaces each category with a 0/1 column that says whether the row is in that category
Replaces each category with its position in an alphabetical list of the categories
Replaces each category with a statistic of the target for that category, such as its mean
questions.explanation: It links the feature value to the target value statistically. The other options describe frequency encoding, one-hot and label encoding.

questions.question: Category 'A' appears in four training rows whose targets are 1, 0, 1 and 1. What is the target-encoded value for A (mean of the target)?
questions.explanation: Three of the four targets are 1, so the mean is 3 / 4 = 0.75.

questions.question: What is the main risk of target encoding?
options: It uses the same number for every category, so it hides all the differences
It uses the answer column, so it can leak the target into the features and overfit
It uses one column for each category, so it makes the table far too wide
It uses the row order, so it gives different results when the rows are shuffled
questions.explanation: Calculate the encoding from the training data only (or inside cross-validation), never from the test rows' targets.

questions.question: A 'postal code' feature has 800 categories. Which encoding avoids adding 800 columns?
options: One-hot encoding, which gives one numeric column
Binary encoding, which gives one column per category
Target encoding, which gives one numeric column
Equal-width binning, which gives one column per category
questions.explanation: High-cardinality features make one-hot very wide. Target encoding stays one column, with the leakage caveat.

questions.question: One-hot encoding adds no false order between the categories.
questions.explanation: Each category gets its own column, so none is bigger than another.

questions.question: Target encoding should be calculated using the target values of the test set.
questions.explanation: That would leak test answers into the features. Learn the encoding from training data only.

questions.question: Match each encoding to the situation it suits.

pairs.right: A feature with two values, such as yes or no
A nominal feature with a handful of categories
A feature with very many categories
A numeric feature turned into ranges

questions.question: The pandas function pd.get_____ () creates one-hot columns. (one word)
questions.explanation: pd.get_dummies(df['colour']) one-hot encodes a column.

questions.question: Why scale numeric features?
options: So features with small values are removed from the model entirely
So features with missing values are filled in with the average
So features with text values are turned into columns of numbers
So features with large values do not dominate those with small values
questions.explanation: A salary in the tens of thousands would swamp an age under 100 in a distance calculation. Scaling puts them on comparable ranges.

questions.question: What is the formula for min-max scaling?
options: (x - min) / (max - min)
(x - mean) / standard deviation
(x - median) / (max - min)
x / (max + min)
questions.explanation: The smallest value becomes 0 and the largest becomes 1. The mean and standard deviation formula is standardization.

questions.question: A column holds 20, 30, 50 and 60. What is 30 after min-max scaling?
A column has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What is the value 70 after standardization?
questions.explanation: (70 - 50) / 10 = 2, meaning two standard deviations above the mean.

questions.question: What are the mean and standard deviation of a standardized column?
options: A mean of 1 and a standard deviation of 0
A mean of 0.5 and a standard deviation of 1
A mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.5
A mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1
questions.explanation: Standardization is also called z-score scaling: the column is re-centred on 0 and measured in standard deviations.

questions.question: What happens to min-max scaling when one value is a huge outlier?
options: The outlier becomes 1 and the other values are squeezed into a narrow band near 0
The outlier becomes 0 and the other values are spread evenly across the range
The outlier is removed and the other values are spread across a wider range
The outlier is ignored and the other values are scaled exactly as they were before
questions.explanation: Min-max uses the extremes, so one extreme value sets the scale for everyone.

questions.question: Compared with min-max scaling, how does standardization treat outliers?
options: It sets a fixed range, so an outlier is forced to equal 1 and the rest are compressed
It sets no fixed range, so an outlier does not compress the rest, though it still moves the mean and spread
It sets no fixed range, so an outlier is deleted and cannot affect the mean or spread
It sets a fixed range, so an outlier is replaced with the median and the rest are unchanged
questions.explanation: Standardized values can be any size, so an outlier simply gets a large z-score. It is less damaging than under min-max, but not harmless.

questions.question: A feature is strongly right-skewed (a long tail of large values). What does scaling do to the skew?
options: It removes the skew, because scaled values are always spread symmetrically
It reverses the skew, because the long tail is moved to the other side
Nothing: scaling changes the range or centre but not the shape of the distribution
It doubles the skew, because the large values are stretched even further
questions.explanation: Both methods are linear, so the shape stays the same. A transform such as log reduces skew.

questions.question: Which type of model is most affected by unscaled features?
options: Decision trees that split on one feature at a time
Random forests that average many such decision trees
Rule lists that test one feature against one threshold
Distance-based models such as kNN
questions.explanation: kNN adds feature differences into one distance, so scale matters. Trees compare one feature at a time, so scale rarely matters.

questions.question: On which data should a scaler learn its minimum, maximum, mean or standard deviation?
options: The training set only, then apply the same numbers to the test set
The test set only, then apply the same numbers to the training set
The full dataset before splitting, so both parts share the same numbers
Each set separately, so that both parts end up with the same distribution
questions.explanation: Fitting on the test set (or the full dataset) leaks information about unseen data into training.

questions.question: A kNN model is built on features whose distribution is unknown and not bell-shaped. Which scaling is the usual choice?
options: Standardization, which needs the data to follow a normal distribution
Min-max scaling, which needs no assumption about the distribution
No scaling, which works because kNN compares one feature at a time
A log transform, which makes every feature follow a normal distribution
questions.explanation: Min-max suits unknown or non-Gaussian data and distance-based models such as kNN or neural networks.

questions.question: When does standardization fit better than min-max scaling?
options: The algorithm needs every value to lie between 0 and 1 exactly
The algorithm compares one feature at a time and ignores the scale
The algorithm assumes the data are roughly normally distributed
The algorithm works on category labels rather than numeric columns
questions.explanation: Standardization centres the data on 0 with a standard deviation of 1, which is what methods assuming a normal distribution expect.

questions.question: Min-max scaling always produces a column with a mean of 0.
questions.explanation: Min-max gives values from 0 to 1, and the mean depends on the data. Standardization is the one that gives mean 0.

questions.question: Standardized values can be negative.
questions.explanation: Values below the column's mean have negative z-scores.

questions.question: Min-max scaling is often called ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Min-max scaling is commonly called normalization.

questions.question: Why is the data split into a training set and a test set?
options: To remove the examples that contain missing or extreme values
To double the number of examples the model learns from
To save time by using fewer features in each of the sets
To measure performance on examples the model has not seen
questions.explanation: A model can look perfect on data it learned from. Only held-back data shows how it generalizes.

questions.question: Which train-test split ratio is generally recommended?
options: About 80% training and 20% test
About 50% training and 50% test
About 95% training and 5% test
About 20% training and 80% test
questions.explanation: 80/20 gives plenty of training data while keeping a test set big enough to be meaningful.

questions.question: A dataset has 250 rows and is split 80/20. How many rows are in the test set?
questions.explanation: 20% of 250 = 50 test rows, leaving 200 for training.

questions.question: A model scores 98% on the training set and 70% on the test set. What does this suggest?
options: Underfitting: it was too simple to capture the pattern in the training data
Good fit: it learned the pattern and generalizes to new data well
Overfitting: it memorized the training data and does not generalize
Leakage: it was given the test labels and used them to score itself
questions.explanation: A large gap between training and test accuracy, with training far higher, is the sign of overfitting.

questions.question: A model scores 61% on the training set and 59% on the test set. What does this suggest?
options: Overfitting: it is too complex, so it does well on one set only
Good fit: it is balanced, so it does equally well on both sets
Leakage: it is too lucky, so it does worse on the set it never saw
Underfitting: it is too simple, so it does poorly on both sets
questions.explanation: Low accuracy on both sets means the model has not captured the pattern.

questions.question: A model scores 91% on training data and 89% on test data. What is the best conclusion?
options: It generalizes well: the two scores are high and close together
It underfits badly: the two scores are close, so it has learned too little
It overfits badly: the two scores are high, so it has memorized the data
It cheats: the two scores differ at all, so it has seen the test data
questions.explanation: Generalization means the training result carries over to unseen data. A small gap with high scores is the goal.

questions.question: A confusion matrix has 30 true positives, 10 false positives, 20 false negatives and 40 true negatives. What is the accuracy?
questions.explanation: Correct predictions are the diagonal: 30 + 40 = 70 out of 100 total.

questions.question: In a confusion matrix, what does a false negative mean?
options: The model predicted positive but the actual class was negative
The model predicted negative and the actual class was negative
The model predicted negative but the actual class was positive
The model predicted positive and the actual class was positive
questions.explanation: The first word says whether the prediction was right; the second is what the model predicted. A false negative is a missed positive.

questions.question: What does k-fold cross-validation do?
options: Splits the data into k parts and uses only the first part as the test set, keeping its score
Splits the data into k parts and trains on the smallest part, averaging the weights
Splits the data into k parts and shuffles them k times, keeping the best score
Splits the data into k parts and uses each part once as the test set, averaging the scores
questions.explanation: Every row is used for testing exactly once and for training k - 1 times.

questions.question: A dataset of 200 rows is used for 5-fold cross-validation. How many rows are in each round's test fold and training set?
options: 40 test rows and 160 training rows
20 test rows and 180 training rows
50 test rows and 150 training rows
40 test rows and 40 training rows
questions.explanation: 200 / 5 = 40 rows per fold. Each round trains on the other four folds: 160 rows.

questions.question: Why can cross-validation be more reliable than a single train-test split?
options: The score does not depend on the training rows, since none are used in it
The score does not depend on one lucky or unlucky choice of test rows
The score does not depend on the model, since the same one is used each time
The score does not depend on the features, since the folds ignore the columns
questions.explanation: Averaging over several different test folds smooths out a single odd split.

questions.question: The test set can be used repeatedly to tune the model's settings without any harm.
questions.explanation: Tuning against the test set makes its score optimistic. Use a validation set or cross-validation for tuning.

questions.question: With 5-fold cross-validation, five models are trained.
questions.explanation: One per round, each tested on a different fold.

questions.question: How well a model performs on new, unseen data is called ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Generalization is the goal: the training result should carry over to unseen data.

questions.question: A model has 99% accuracy on the training set and 64% on the test set. Explain what is wrong, how the two numbers show it, and name two things you might try.
questions.modelAnswer: The model is overfitting: it has memorized the training examples, including their noise, so it does not generalize. The warning sign is the large gap, with training accuracy far above test accuracy. Fixes include using a simpler model or a smaller number of features, getting more training data, or using cross-validation to choose settings that generalize.
rubric: Names the problem as overfitting (memorizing the training data)
Uses the gap between the training and test accuracy as the evidence
Gives at least one reasonable fix, such as a simpler model, fewer features or more data
Says that the test score is the better estimate of real-world performance

questions.question: What is the curse of dimensionality?
options: Problems that grow as the number of rows increases, such as slower sorting and memory use
Problems that grow as the number of classes decreases, such as a lack of variety in the targets
Problems that grow as the number of features increases, such as sparse data and rising cost
Problems that grow as the number of missing values increases, such as biased averages
questions.explanation: Dimensions are features. More of them makes the space larger and the data thinner.

questions.question: What happens to the data as features are added while the number of rows stays the same?
options: The rows pack together in a much smaller space, so the data becomes dense
The rows stay equally spread in the same space, so the data stays the same
The rows merge with their neighbours in a smaller space, so the data shrinks
The rows spread out through a much larger space, so the data becomes sparse
questions.explanation: Each new feature multiplies the volume of the space, so the same number of points covers less of it.

questions.question: How does high dimensionality affect distance-based methods such as kNN?
options: Distances between points become similar, so 'nearest' neighbours are less meaningful
Distances between points become exact, so the nearest neighbours are easier to find
Distances between points become zero, so the nearest neighbours are all identical
Distances between points are unchanged, so the nearest neighbours are equally clear
questions.explanation: In many dimensions nearly every point is about as far from the query as every other.

questions.question: How does adding many features usually change the risk of overfitting?
options: It falls, because the model has more information to separate the noise from the signal
It rises, because the model has more ways to fit the noise in the training data
It stays the same, because the model ignores features that do not help it
It falls to zero, because the model can describe each row in more detail
questions.explanation: With many features and few rows, a model can often find a pattern that is only noise.

questions.question: What generally happens to the amount of data needed to cover the feature space well as features are added?
options: It grows slowly, roughly in proportion to the features
It stays fixed, regardless of how many features there are
It grows very fast, roughly exponentially
It shrinks, because each feature provides more clues about the target
questions.explanation: Covering the space at the same density takes many times more points for each extra dimension.

questions.question: Besides accuracy, what else gets worse as the number of features climbs?
options: Training time and memory use, because there is less to compute and store
Test accuracy and training accuracy, because both always fall with more columns
Number of rows and missing values, because both always rise with more columns
Training time and memory use, because there is more to compute and store
questions.explanation: Complexity and cost rise with dimensionality; a bigger model is also harder to interpret.

questions.question: Which action is a standard remedy for the curse of dimensionality?
options: Feature selection or dimensionality reduction such as PCA
Adding more columns until the model has enough detail
Filling the missing values in every column with the mean
Raising the training share of the split from 80% to 99%
questions.explanation: Both remove or combine features so the model works in a smaller space.

questions.question: A table has 100 rows and 500 features. Which concern is the most pressing?
options: There are far more rows than features, so underfitting is very likely
There are far more features than rows, so overfitting is very likely
There are as many rows as features, so the model must be too simple
There are no categorical features, so the model cannot be trained
questions.explanation: With so few rows in such a large space, a model can memorize the training data.

questions.question: Adding more features always improves a model's accuracy.
questions.explanation: Useless or redundant features can add noise and cost, and past a point accuracy can get worse.

questions.question: One-hot encoding a column with hundreds of categories raises the number of dimensions a great deal.
questions.explanation: It adds one column per category, which can feed the curse of dimensionality.

questions.question: The problems of sparse data and rising cost that come with many features are called the curse of ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Dimensionality is the number of features.

questions.question: What is a filter method of feature selection?
options: It repeatedly trains a model on different feature subsets and keeps the subset with the best score
It reads the weights or importances from a model that has already been trained and drops the low ones
It scores features with simple statistics, such as correlation, and drops the weak ones before any model is trained
It combines the original features into a few new ones that keep as much of the variation as possible
questions.explanation: Filters are fast and independent of any model. The other options describe wrapper, embedded and PCA.

questions.question: What is a wrapper method of feature selection?
options: It scores each feature with a simple statistic and drops the weak ones before any model is trained
It reads weights or importances from one trained model and drops the features with the lowest ones
It combines the original features into a few new ones that keep as much of the variation as possible
It trains a model on feature subsets over and over and uses an evaluation score to decide which to keep
questions.explanation: Recursive feature elimination (RFE) is an example. It is accurate for the chosen model but expensive, since many models are trained.

questions.question: What is an embedded method of feature selection?
options: It uses the results of a model, such as coefficients or importances, to decide which features to remove
It tests feature subsets with repeated training runs and an evaluation score to choose the best set
It ranks features with simple statistics like correlation and removes the weak ones before training
It merges the original features into a few new ones that keep as much of the variation as possible
questions.explanation: Examples: Lasso regression shrinking some coefficients to zero, and the importance scores of a decision tree.

questions.question: Two features have a correlation coefficient of 0.97 with each other. What does this suggest?
options: They are nearly unrelated, so both of them should be kept
They are nearly redundant, so one of them can usually be dropped
They are nearly identical to the target, so both should be kept
They are nearly random noise, so both of them should be dropped
questions.explanation: Highly correlated features carry the same information. Keeping both adds cost without adding much.

questions.question: A feature has a correlation coefficient of 0.02 with the target. What does this suggest?
options: Strong positive relationship with the target, so it is a candidate to keep
Strong negative relationship with the target, so it is a candidate to keep
Little straight-line relationship with the target, so it is a candidate to drop
Perfect redundancy with another feature, so it is a candidate to merge
questions.explanation: A coefficient near 0 means almost no linear relationship. It could still have a non-linear one, so it is a hint, not a proof.

questions.question: A feature has a correlation of -0.85 with the target. How should it be treated?
options: As weakly related to the target, because a negative coefficient means a poor feature
As unrelated to the target, because the minus sign cancels the strength of the link
As redundant with the target, because correlations below zero repeat the target
As strongly related to the target, because the size of the coefficient is what matters
questions.explanation: A negative sign only means that the two move in opposite directions. -0.85 is as strong as +0.85.

questions.question: What does SelectKBest(k=5) do?
options: Scores each feature against the target and keeps the five with the highest scores
Scores each pair of features against each other and keeps the five least related
Scores each row against the target and keeps the five rows that fit the best
Scores each class against the features and keeps the five most common classes
questions.explanation: It is a univariate filter method: one score per feature, then the top k.

questions.question: What does 'univariate' mean in univariate feature selection?
options: Each feature is judged together with all the others, as a combined group
Each feature is judged on its own against the target, ignoring the others
Each feature is judged against the others, ignoring the target entirely
Each feature is judged on one training row at a time, ignoring the rest
questions.explanation: The weakness is that it can miss features that are only useful in combination.

questions.question: Which approach usually costs the most computing time?
options: A filter method, because it trains a model for every feature it scores
An embedded method, because it trains a model for every subset it tries
A wrapper method, because it trains a model for every subset it tries
A correlation check, because it trains a model for every pair it compares
questions.explanation: Filters are cheapest, embedded methods piggyback on a single training run, and wrappers train many models.

questions.question: What does forward feature selection do?
options: Starts with every feature and removes the one that helps least, one at a time
Starts with no features and adds all of them whose correlation passes a cut-off
Starts with every feature and keeps the ones a single fitted model rates highest
Starts with no features and adds the one that helps most, one at a time
questions.explanation: Forward selection and backward elimination are both wrapper methods. They score each step by training a model.

questions.question: What does backward feature elimination do?
options: Starts with every feature and removes the weakest one, one at a time
Starts with no features and adds the strongest one, one at a time
Starts with every feature and removes all of the weak ones in one step
Starts with no features and adds the ones that are the least correlated
questions.explanation: Each round refits the model without one feature and drops the one whose removal hurts the score least.

questions.question: What does an exhaustive feature search do?
options: Tries every pair of features and keeps the pair with the highest correlation
Tries every possible combination of features and keeps the best-scoring set
Tries every feature on its own and keeps the one with the strongest score
Tries every model type on the full set and keeps the one with the best score
questions.explanation: It is the most thorough wrapper approach, but the number of combinations explodes as features are added.

questions.question: Why might a feature with very low variance be dropped by a filter method?
options: Its values differ greatly between rows, so it is likely to add noise to the target
Its values repeat another column exactly, so it is certain to hold the same information
Its values barely differ between rows, so it is unlikely to help predict the target
Its values are missing in most rows, so it is impossible to give the model any signal
questions.explanation: A column that is nearly constant cannot separate one outcome from another. Histograms and bar charts show this quickly.

questions.question: How often does an embedded method fit the model, compared with a wrapper method?
options: Many times, which makes it dearer than a wrapper that fits a single time
Never, which makes it quicker than a filter that scores the features directly
Once per feature, which makes it the same cost as a wrapper in every case
Once, which makes it cheaper than a wrapper that refits for every subset
questions.explanation: An embedded method such as Lasso selects features as a side effect of one training run, so it balances speed against effectiveness.

questions.question: Match each approach to an example.

pairs.right: Dropping features whose correlation with the target is near zero
Recursive feature elimination, repeatedly refitting a model
Lasso shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero
A table of correlations between every pair of features

questions.question: Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features without changing them.
questions.explanation: That is how it differs from PCA, which builds new features.

questions.question: A feature-selection method that repeatedly trains a model on subsets and judges each by an evaluation metric is called a ____ method. (one word)
questions.explanation: Filter methods use simple criteria, wrapper methods use a model's score, and embedded methods use a model's own results.

questions.question: Describe the three approaches to feature selection (filter, wrapper, embedded). For each, give one example and one point of comparison.
questions.modelAnswer: Filter: scores features with simple criteria such as correlation with the target, independent of any model; it is fast but ignores how features work together. Wrapper: repeatedly trains a model on different subsets and keeps what scores best, as in recursive feature elimination; it tends to find a good set for that model but is expensive. Embedded: uses the results of a model, such as Lasso coefficients or tree importances, to pick features during training; it is cheaper than a wrapper but depends on the chosen model.
rubric: Describes the filter approach with an example (correlation or a statistical test)
Describes the wrapper approach with an example (such as RFE)
Describes the embedded approach with an example (such as Lasso or tree importances)
Compares them, for example on speed or dependence on a model

questions.question: What does principal component analysis (PCA) do?
options: Builds a smaller set of new, uncorrelated features that keep as much of the variation as possible
Picks a smaller set of the original features that have the highest correlation with the target
Builds a larger set of new, correlated features that describe the same variation more simply
Picks a smaller set of rows that are the most typical of each class in the training data
questions.explanation: PCA is dimensionality reduction by transformation, not by choosing columns.

questions.question: Which direction does the first principal component point along?
options: The direction in which the data varies the least
The direction in which the data varies the most
The direction in which the target is most correlated
The direction in which the data is most evenly spread
questions.explanation: Later components capture the most remaining variation, at right angles to the earlier ones.

questions.question: How are the principal components related to each other?
options: They are parallel to each other, so they are fully correlated
They are copies of each other, so they are fully redundant
They are perpendicular to each other, so they are uncorrelated
They are tied to the target, so they are fully predictive
questions.explanation: Each component is orthogonal to the others, so it adds information the others do not have.

questions.question: Does PCA use the target variable?
options: Yes: it picks components by how well they predict the target, so it is supervised
Yes: it needs the target to scale the features, so it is semi-supervised
No: it looks only at the rows, so it is a type of reinforcement learning
No: it looks only at the features, so it is an unsupervised technique
questions.explanation: PCA finds directions of variance in the features alone, which may or may not be useful for predicting the target.

questions.question: Why are features usually standardized before PCA?
options: A feature with a large scale would otherwise dominate the variance and the components
A feature with a small scale would otherwise be dropped before the components are found
A feature with missing values would otherwise be filled with the mean automatically
A feature with text values would otherwise be turned into a number automatically
questions.explanation: PCA chases variance, and variance depends on units. Scaling gives every feature an equal chance.

questions.question: Components explain 60%, 25%, 10% and 5% of the variance. How many are needed to keep at least 90%?
questions.explanation: 60 + 25 = 85%, which is short of 90%. Adding the third (10%) gives 95%.

questions.question: What is a drawback of using PCA components as features?
options: Each component repeats one original feature, so the model learns nothing new
Each component adds many new features, so the model has more data to process
Each component mixes many original features, so the model is harder to interpret
Each component needs the target, so the model has less data to test on
questions.explanation: A component is a weighted blend of the original columns, which no longer have their original meaning.

questions.question: How does PCA differ from filter-style feature selection?
options: PCA keeps some originals unchanged, while selection creates new features from combinations
PCA needs the target to score each column, while selection ignores the target completely
PCA drops rows that carry little variance, while selection drops columns that carry none
PCA creates new features from combinations, while selection keeps some originals unchanged
questions.explanation: Selection removes columns. PCA replaces the columns with new ones.

questions.question: A table has 10 features. PCA is run and 3 components are kept. How many columns does the transformed data have?
questions.explanation: The data is rebuilt using only the kept components, one column per component.

questions.question: The components found by PCA are ordered, with the first explaining the most variance.
questions.explanation: Each later component explains no more of the variance than the one before it.

questions.question: PCA removes the need to standardize, because it works the same on any scale.
questions.explanation: PCA is sensitive to scale, so features are normally standardized first.

questions.question: The share of the total variance that one principal component captures is called its explained variance ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: In scikit-learn, pca.explained_variance_ratio_ lists the share for each component.

questions.question: Explain what PCA does and why it is used. Give one benefit and one cost of using it.
questions.modelAnswer: PCA turns the original features into a smaller set of new features called principal components. They are uncorrelated, and the first captures the most variance, the next the most of what remains, and so on. Keeping only the first few reduces the number of features, which helps with the curse of dimensionality, speed and overfitting. The cost is interpretability, because each component is a blend of the original features, and information in the dropped components is lost. Features are usually standardized first.
rubric: Says PCA builds new features (components) from combinations of the originals
Says components are ordered by the variance they capture
Gives a benefit, such as fewer dimensions, speed or less overfitting
Gives a cost, such as lost interpretability or lost variance
